summary: Defines a new RTCP Extended Report block type for post-repair loss, using run length encoding. It reports which RTP packets are still lost after repair mechanisms such as retransmission or forward error correction have been applied. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: After fixing missing pieces of a video, you want to know which pieces are still missing. This report block tells the sender that, in a short compact form.

how to report packet loss after repair in rtcp

subtitle: An RTCP report block that tells a sender which RTP packets were still missing after every repair method had run.

tldr.problem: The existing RTCP Loss RLE report is collected before any loss repair, so it cannot show which lost packets were recovered by FEC or retransmission and which are still missing.
tldr.mechanism: A new XR report block, the Post-repair Loss RLE, uses the same layout as the Loss RLE and reports the packets still lost after all loss-repair methods. It has block type 10, and an SDP parameter, post-repair-loss-rle, signals it.
tldr.outcome: Comparing pre-repair and post-repair reports lets a sender or monitor judge how well loss repair worked in aggregate. Partially repaired packets count as unrepaired.

today: RFC 5725 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the Loss RLE block of RFC 3611.

sections.title: Why a Post-Repair Report
sections.content:
RTCP is the control protocol that accompanies RTP media streams, and RTCP Extended Reports (XRs) from RFC 3611 add more detailed reports. One of them is the Loss RLE report block, which describes individual packet receipts and losses over the RTCP interval before the report was sent.

That report is usually collected on the primary source stream before any repair. Loss-repair methods such as forward error correction (RFC 5109) or retransmission (RFC 4588) may recover some lost packets, but the pre-repair report cannot show which ones, so it cannot show how well repair performed.

This RFC fixes that with a second block, the Post-repair Loss RLE, which reports the source packets that remain missing.
sections.eli5: A first report says which video pieces went missing. A second report says which are still missing after you tried to fix them.

sections.title: Comparing Before and After
sections.content:
When the pre-repair and post-repair reports are compared, the RTP sender or another third-party entity can judge the loss-repair methods in aggregate. To avoid ambiguity, it is RECOMMENDED that the post-repair report cover source packets that have no further chance of repair. If repair may still recover packets, the report SHOULD NOT be sent until recovery is complete.

The wait cannot be unlimited. Sequence-number wrapping in the primary stream could make a late report ambiguous, so Post-repair Loss RLE reports may not be delayed arbitrarily. If the reports are ambiguous, the sender or monitor must work out which packets a report refers to.

Like the pre-repair report, it works at packet level and counts partially repaired packets as unrepaired. Methods that only partially recover data SHOULD NOT be evaluated with it, since that may underestimate their effectiveness. The RFC only considers reporting after all repair methods have been applied, not after each method in a hybrid system.

Applications MAY report for every received packet or only for a set of specific packets, so coverage need not be contiguous.
sections.eli5: Wait until you have finished fixing before you report what is still broken. If you wait too long, nobody can tell which pieces the report is about.

sections.title: The Report Block Format
sections.content:
The block deliberately uses the same structure as the Loss RLE block in RFC 3611, so implementations can compare the two efficiently. Its fields are:

  • BT (8 bits): the constant 10 identifies a Post-repair Loss RLE block.
  • rsvd. (4 bits): reserved, MUST be set to zero and MUST be ignored by the receiver.
  • T, thinning (4 bits): only packets with sequence numbers 0 mod 2^T are reported. 0 means no thinning. The maximum thinning is one packet in every 32,768.
  • block length (16 bits): the length of the block including the header, in 32-bit words minus one.
  • SSRC of source (32 bits): the RTP source being reported on.
  • begin_seq and end_seq (16 bits each): the first sequence number reported, and the last one plus one.
  • chunk 1 to chunk n (16 bits each): defined in Section 4 of RFC 3611. An all-zero chunk is a terminating null chunk. Otherwise the left-most bit gives the type, 0 for run length and 1 for bit vector.

If thinning is used, it is RECOMMENDED to use the same value in the pre-repair and post-repair reports, though different values MAY be used. The sequence numbers refer to the primary source stream. The bandwidth usage rules of RFC 3611 apply here as well.
sections.eli5: The report is a short form with a label saying what it is, which stream it is about, the range of packet numbers, and a compact list of which ones are missing.

sections.title: Signaling in SDP
sections.content:
Endpoints announce support in the Session Description Protocol through a new parameter of the rtcp-xr attribute. The syntax, in ABNF, is pkt-loss-rle-post = "post-repair-loss-rle" ["=" max-size], where max-size is one or more digits giving the maximum block size in octets.

The full syntax of the rtcp-xr attribute is in Section 5.1 of RFC 3611, and the new parameter is compatible with its format-ext definition.
sections.eli5: Before a call, each side can say in its setup note that it is willing to send these reports, and how big they may get.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3611 apply. The RFC adds that an attacker who watches pre-repair reports from receivers in a multicast network may infer network characteristics, but post-repair reports reveal nothing more, and without the pre-repair reports they are of no use to an attacker. They only show how effective repair was, which an attacker could work out from watching the RTP packets and running the repair algorithms.

An attacker interfering with repair could see from the reports whether the attack works. The RFC says this does not pose a security risk in practice. A forged report in either block could mislead the sender's proactive or reactive repair decisions, so a sender application should be aware of this and take precautions. Like other RTCP XR reports, the block MAY be protected with SRTP and SRTCP.
sections.eli5: The report mostly tells a spy what they could have worked out anyway. The bigger worry is someone sending a fake report to confuse the sender, so senders should be careful.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC assigns block type value 10 in the RTCP XR Block Type Registry to the Post-repair Loss RLE Report Block. It also registers the SDP parameter post-repair-loss-rle for the rtcp-xr attribute in the RTCP XR SDP Parameters Registry. General guidance for new XR block types is in RFC 3611.
sections.eli5: The number 10 and the name for this report were written in the official list so nobody else uses them for something different.

fields.name: rsvd.
fields.desc: Reserved; set to zero and ignored by the receiver.

fields.name: T
fields.desc: Thinning of the sequence-number space; 0 means none.

fields.name: block length
fields.desc: Block length in 32-bit words minus one.

fields.name: SSRC of source
fields.desc: The RTP source being reported on.

fields.name: end_seq
fields.desc: Last sequence number reported plus one.

fields.name: chunk 1
fields.desc: Run length, bit vector or terminating null chunk.

fields.name: chunk 2
fields.desc: Further chunks follow up to chunk n.

data.title: ABNF
data.code:
pkt-loss-rle-post = "post-repair-loss-rle" ["=" max-size]

max-size = 1*DIGIT ; maximum block size in octets
